entries.aa584db011a6920731643e0aff768b2eaa0ad947: <div sID="gen12099" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="90" osisID="Ps.90" sID="Ps.90"/> <div eID="gen12099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12100" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12101" type="x-p"/> The foregoing psalm is supposed to have been penned as late as the captivity in Babylon; this, it is plain, was penned as early as the deliverance out of Egypt, and yet they are put close together in this collection of divine songs. This psalm was penned by Moses (as appears by the title), the most ancient penman of sacred writ. We have upon record a praising song of his (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.1-Exod.15.21">Exod. xv.</reference>, which is alluded to <reference osisRef="Rev.15.3">Rev. xv. 3</reference>), and an instructing song of his, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.1-Deut.32.47">Deut. xxxii.</reference> But this is of a different nature from both, for it is called a prayer. It is supposed that this psalm was penned upon occasion of the sentence passed upon Israel in the wilderness for their unbelief, murmuring, and rebellion, that their carcases should fall in the wilderness, that they should be wasted away by a series of miseries for thirty-eight years together, and that none of them that were then of age should enter Canaan. This was calculated for their wanderings in the wilderness, as that other song of Moses (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.19">Deut. xxxi. 19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">21</reference>) was for their settlement in Canaan. We have the story to which this psalm seems to refer, <reference osisRef="Num.14.1-Num.14.45">Num. xiv.</reference> Probably Moses penned this prayer to be daily used, either by the people in their tents, or, at lest, by the priests in the tabernacle-service, during their tedious fatigue in the wilderness. In it, I. Moses comforts himself and his people with the eternity of God and their interest in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1-Ps.90.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. He humbles himself and his people with the consideration of the frailty of man, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.3-Ps.90.6">ver. 3-6</reference>. III. He submits himself and his people to the righteous sentence of God passed upon them, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.7-Ps.90.11">ver. 7-11</reference>. IV. He commits himself and his people to God by prayer for divine mercy and grace, and the return of God's favour, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.12-Ps.90.17">ver. 12-17</reference>. Though it seems to have been penned upon this particular occasion, yet it is very applicable to the frailty of human life in general, and, in singing it, we may easily apply it to the years of our passage through the wilderness of this world, and it furnishes us with meditations and prayers very suitable to the solemnity of a funeral.
entries.b2b9e760e854be8332b085db2e4ec1874b45a115: <div eID="gen12101" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12100" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Care of His People; Frailty of Human Life.</title> <div sID="gen12102" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations. <hi type="super">2</hi> Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> God. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thou turnest man to destruction; and sayest, Return, ye children of men. 4 For a thousand years in thy sight <hi type="italic">are but</hi> as yesterday when it is past, and <hi type="italic">as</hi> a watch in the night. 5 Thou carriest them away as with a flood; they are <hi type="italic">as</hi> a sleep: in the morning <hi type="italic">they are</hi> like grass <hi type="italic">which</hi> groweth up. <hi type="super">6</hi> In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth. <div eID="gen12102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12103" type="x-p"/> This psalm is entitled <hi type="italic">a prayer of Moses.</hi> Where, and in what volume, it was preserved from Moses's time till the collection of psalms was begun to be made, is uncertain; but, being divinely inspired, it was under a special protection: perhaps it was written in the book of Jasher, or the book of the wars of the Lord. Moses taught the people of Israel to pray, and put words into their mouths which they might make use of in turning to the Lord. Moses is here called <hi type="italic">the man of God,</hi> because he was a prophet, the father of prophets, and an eminent type of the great prophet. In these verses we are taught, <div eID="gen12103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12104" type="x-p"/> I. To give God the praise of his care concerning his people at all times, and concerning us in our days (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lord, thou hast been to us a habitation,</hi> or <hi type="italic">dwelling-place, a refuge</hi> or <hi type="italic">help, in all generations.</hi> Now that they had fallen under God's displeasure, and he threatened to abandon them, they plead his former kindnesses to their ancestors. Canaan was a land of pilgrimage to their fathers the patriarchs, who dwelt there in tabernacles; but then God was their habitation, and, wherever they went, they were at home, at rest, in him. Egypt had been a land of bondage to them for many years, but even then God was their refuge; and in him that poor oppressed people lived and were kept in being. Note, True believers are at home in God, and that is their comfort in reference to all the toils and tribulations they meet with in this world. In him we may repose and shelter ourselves as in our dwelling-place. <div eID="gen12104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12105" type="x-p"/> II. To give God the glory of his eternity (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Before the mountains were brought forth, before he made the highest part of the dust of the world</hi> (as it is expressed, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.26">Prov. viii. 26</reference>), <hi type="italic">before the earth fell in travail,</hi> or, as we may read it, <hi type="italic">before thou hadst formed the earth and the world</hi> (that is, before the beginning of time) thou hadst a being; <hi type="italic">even from everlasting to everlasting thou art God,</hi> an eternal God, whose existence has neither its commencement nor its period with time, nor is measured by the successions and revolutions of it, but who art <hi type="italic">the same yesterday, to-day, and for ever,</hi> without beginning of days, or end of life, or change of time. Note, Against all the grievances that arise from our own mortality, and the mortality of our friends, we may take comfort from God's immortality. We are dying creatures, and all our comforts in the world are dying comforts, but God is an everliving God, and those shall find him so who have him for theirs. <div eID="gen12105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12106" type="x-p"/> III. To own God's absolute sovereign dominion over man, and his irresistible incontestable power to dispose of him as he pleases (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou turnest man to destruction,</hi> with a word's speaking, when thou pleasest, to the destruction of the body, of the earthly house; <hi type="italic">and</hi> thou <hi type="italic">sayest, Return, you children of men.</hi> 1. When God is, by sickness or other afflictions, turning men to destruction, he does thereby call men to return unto him, that is, to repent of their sins and live a new life. This God <hi type="italic">speaketh once, yea, twice. "Return unto me,</hi> from whom you have revolted," <reference osisRef="Jer.4.1">Jer. iv. 1</reference>. 2. When God is threatening to <hi type="italic">turn men to destruction,</hi> to bring them to death, and they have received a sentence of death within themselves, sometimes he wonderfully restores them, and says, as the old translation reads it, <hi type="italic">Again thou sayest, Return</hi> to life and health again. For God kills and makes alive again, brings down to the grave and brings up. 3. When God turns men to destruction, it is according to the general sentence passed upon all, which is this, "<hi type="italic">Return, you children of men,</hi> one, as well as another, return to your first principles; let the body return to the earth as it was (<hi type="italic">dust to dust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.3.19">Gen. iii. 19</reference>) and let the soul <hi type="italic">return to God who gave it,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.7">Eccl. xii. 7</reference>. 4. Though God turns all men to destruction, yet he will again say, <hi type="italic">Return, you children of men,</hi> at the general resurrection, when, though a man dies, yet he shall live again; and "<hi type="italic">then shalt thou call and I will answer</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.14.14-Job.14.15">Job xiv. 14, 15</reference>); thou shalt bid me return, and I shall return." The body, the soul, shall both return and unite again. <div eID="gen12106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12107" type="x-p"/> IV. To acknowledge the infinite disproportion there is between God and men, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.4">v. 4</reference>. Some of the patriarchs lived nearly a thousand years; Moses knew this very well, and had recorded it: but what is their long life to God's eternal life? "A thousand years, to us, are a long period, which we cannot expect to survive; or, if we could, it is what we could not retain the remembrance of; but it is, <hi type="italic">in thy sight, as yesterday,</hi> as one day, as that which is freshest in mind; nay, it is but as a <hi type="italic">watch of the night,</hi>" which was but three hours. 1. A thousand years are nothing to God's eternity; they are less than a day, than an hour, to a thousand years. Betwixt a minute and a million of years there is some proportion, but betwixt time and eternity there is none. The long lives of the patriarchs were nothing to God, not so much as the life of a child (that is born and dies the same day) is to theirs. 2. All the events of a thousand years, whether past or to come, are as present to the Eternal Mind as what was done yesterday, or the last hour, is to us, and more so. God will say, at the great day, to those whom he has <hi type="italic">turned to destruction, Return—Arise you dead.</hi> But it might be objected against the doctrine of the resurrection that it is a long time since it was expected and it has not yet come. Let that be no difficulty, for a thousand years, in God's sight, are but as one day. <hi type="italic">Nullum tempus occurrit regi—To the king all periods are alike.</hi> To this purport these words are quoted, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.8">2 Pet. iii. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen12107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12108" type="x-p"/> V. To see the frailty of man, and his vanity even at his best estate (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.5-Ps.90.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): look upon all the children of men, and we shall see, 1. That their life is a dying life: <hi type="italic">Thou carriest them away as with a flood,</hi> that is, they are continually gliding down the stream of time into the ocean of eternity. The flood is continually flowing, and they are carried away with it; as soon as we are born we begin to die, and every day of our life carries us so much nearer death; or we are carried away violently and irresistibly, as with a flood of waters, as with an inundation, which sweeps away all before it; or as the old world was carried away with Noah's flood. Though God promised not so to drown the world again, yet death is a constant deluge. 2. That it is a dreaming life. Men are carried away as with a flood and yet <hi type="italic">they are as a sleep;</hi> they consider not their own frailty, nor are aware how near they approach to an awful eternity. Like men asleep, they imagine great things to themselves, till death wakes them, and puts an end to the pleasing dream. Time passes unobserved by us, as it does with men asleep; and, when it is over, it is as nothing. 3. That it is a short and transient life, like that of the grass which grows up and flourishes, in the morning looks green and pleasant, but in the evening the mower cuts it down, and it immediately withers, changes its colour, and loses all its beauty. Death will change us shortly, perhaps suddenly; and it is a great change that death will make with us in a little time. Man, in his prime, does but flourish as the grass, which is weak, and low, and tender, and exposed, and which, when the winter of old age comes, will wither of itself: but he may be mown down by disease or disaster, as the grass is, in the midst of summer. <hi type="italic">All flesh is as grass.</hi>
entries.e65eba19a5c1bca0b5d6baa5b3ad28efed704fd6: <div eID="gen12108" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Penitent Submission.</title> <div sID="gen12109" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> For we are consumed by thine anger, and by thy wrath are we troubled. <hi type="super">8</hi> Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret <hi type="italic">sins</hi> in the light of thy countenance. 9 For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale <hi type="italic">that is told.</hi> <hi type="super">10</hi> The days of our years <hi type="italic">are</hi> threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength <hi type="italic">they be</hi> fourscore years, yet <hi type="italic">is</hi> their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away. <hi type="super">11</hi> Who knoweth the power of thine anger? even according to thy fear, <hi type="italic">so is</hi> thy wrath. <div eID="gen12109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12110" type="x-p"/> Moses had, in the <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1-Ps.90.6">foregoing verses</reference>, lamented the frailty of human life in general; the children of men <hi type="italic">are as a sleep and as the grass.</hi> But here he teaches the people of Israel to confess before God that righteous sentence of death which they were under in a special manner, and which by their sins they had brought upon themselves. Their share in the common lot of mortality was not enough, but they are, and must live and die, under peculiar tokens of God's displeasure. Here they speak of themselves: <hi type="italic">We</hi> Israelites <hi type="italic">are consumed and troubled,</hi> and <hi type="italic">our days have passed away.</hi> <div eID="gen12110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12111" type="x-p"/> I. They are here taught to acknowledge the wrath of God to be the cause of all their miseries. <hi type="italic">We are consumed, we are troubled,</hi> and it is <hi type="italic">by thy anger,</hi> by <hi type="italic">thy wrath</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.7">v. 7</reference>); <hi type="italic">our days have passed away in thy wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.90.9">v. 9</reference>. The afflictions of the saints often come purely from God's love, as Job's; but the rebukes of sinners, and of good men for their sins, must be seen coming from the anger of God, who takes notice of, and is much displeased with, the sins of Israel. We are too apt to look upon death as no more than a debt owing to nature; whereas it is not so; if the nature of man had continued in its primitive purity and rectitude, there would have been no such debt owing to it. It is a debt to the justice of God, a debt to the law. <hi type="italic">Sin entered into the world, and death by sin.</hi> Are we consumed by decays of nature, the infirmities of age, or any chronic disease? We must ascribe it to God's anger. Are we troubled by any sudden or surprising stroke? That also is the fruit of God's wrath, which is thus revealed from heaven against the <hi type="italic">ungodliness</hi> and <hi type="italic">unrighteousness of men.</hi> <div eID="gen12111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12112" type="x-p"/> II. They are taught to confess their sins, which had provoked the wrath of God against them (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, even our secret sins.</hi> It was not without cause that God was angry with them. He had said, <hi type="italic">Provoke me not, and I will do you no hurt;</hi> but they had provoked him, and will own that, in passing this severe sentence upon them, he justly punished them, 1. For their open contempts of him and the daring affronts they had given him: <hi type="italic">Thou hast set our iniquities before thee.</hi> God had herein an eye to their unbelief and murmuring, their distrusting his power and their despising the pleasant land: these he set before them when he passed that sentence on them; these kindled the fire of God's wrath against them and kept good things from them. 2. For their more secret departures from him: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast set our secret sins</hi> (those which go no further than the heart, and which are at the bottom of all the overt acts) <hi type="italic">in the light of thy countenance;</hi> that is, thou hast discovered these, and brought these also to the account, and made us to see them, who before overlooked them." Secret sins are known to God and shall be reckoned for. Those who in heart return into Egypt, who set up idols in their heart, shall be dealt with as revolters or idolaters. See the folly of those who go about to cover their sins, for they cannot cover them. <div eID="gen12112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12113" type="x-p"/> III. They are taught to look upon themselves as dying and passing away, and not to think either of a long life or of a pleasant one; for the decree gone forth against them was irreversible (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">All our days are</hi> likely to be <hi type="italic">passed away in thy wrath,</hi> under the tokens of thy displeasure; and, though we are not quite deprived of the residue of our years, yet we are likely to <hi type="italic">spend</hi> them <hi type="italic">as a tale that is told.</hi> The thirty-eight years which, after this, they wore away in the wilderness, were not the subject of the sacred history; for little or nothing is recorded of that which happened to them from the second year to the fortieth. After they came out of Egypt their time was perfectly trifled away, and was not worthy to be the subject of a history, but only of <hi type="italic">a tale that is told;</hi> for it was only to pass away time, like telling stories, that they spent those years in the wilderness; all that while they were in the consuming, and another generation was in the raising. When they came out of Egypt <hi type="italic">there was not one feeble person among their tribes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.37">Ps. cv. 37</reference>); but now they were feeble. Their joyful prospect of a prosperous glorious life in Canaan was turned into the melancholy prospect of a tedious inglorious death in the wilderness; so that their whole life was now as impertinent a thing as ever any winter-tale was. That is applicable to the state of every one of us in the wilderness of this world: <hi type="italic">We spend our years, we bring them to an end,</hi> each year, and all at last, <hi type="italic">as a tale that is told—as the breath of our mouth in winter</hi> (so some), which soon disappears—<hi type="italic">as a thought</hi> (so some), than which nothing more quick—<hi type="italic">as a word,</hi> which is soon spoken, and then vanishes into air—or <hi type="italic">as a tale that is told.</hi> The spending of our years is like the telling of a tale. A year, when it past, is like a tale when it is told. Some of our years are a pleasant story, others as a tragical one, most mixed, but all short and transient: that which was long in the doing may be told in a short time. Our years, when they are gone, can no more be recalled than the word that we have spoken can. The loss and waste of our time, which are our fault and folly, may be thus complained of: we should spend our years like the despatch of business, with care and industry; but, alas! we do spend them like the telling of a tale, idle, and to little purpose, carelessly, and without regard. Every year passed <hi type="italic">as a tale that is told;</hi> but what was the number of them? As they were vain, so they were few (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.10">v. 10</reference>), seventy or eighty at most, which may be understood either, 1. Of the lives of the Israelites in the wilderness; all those that were numbered when they came out of Egypt, above twenty years old, were to die within thirty-eight years; they numbered those only that <hi type="italic">were able to go forth to war,</hi> most of whom, we may suppose, were between twenty and forty, who therefore must have all died before eighty years old, and many before sixty, and perhaps much sooner, which was far short of the years of the lives of their fathers. And those that lived to seventy or eighty, yet, being under a sentence of consumption and a melancholy despair of ever seeing through this wilderness-state, their strength, their life, was nothing but <hi type="italic">labour and sorrow,</hi> which otherwise would have been made a new life by the joys of Canaan. See what work sin made. Or, 2. Of the lives of men in general, ever since the days of Moses. Before the time of Moses it was usual for men to live about 100 years, or nearly 150; but, since, seventy or eighty is the common stint, which few exceed and multitudes never come near. We reckon those to have lived to the age of man, and to have had as large a share of life as they had reason to expect, who live to be seventy years old; and how short a time is that compared with eternity! Moses was the first that committed divine revelation to writing, which, before, had been transmitted by tradition; now also both the world and the church were pretty well peopled, and therefore there were not now the same reasons for men's living long that there had been. If, by reason of a strong constitution, some reach to eighty years, yet their strength then is what they have little joy of; it does but serve to prolong their misery, and make their death the more tedious; for even <hi type="italic">their strength then is labour and sorrow,</hi> much more their weakness; for the years have come which they have no pleasure in. Or it may be taken thus: <hi type="italic">Our years are seventy, and the years of some, by reason of strength, are eighty; but the breadth of our years</hi> (for so the latter word signifies, rather than strength), <hi type="italic">the whole extent of them, from infancy to old age, is but labour and sorrow.</hi> In the sweat of our face we must eat bread; our whole life is toilsome and troublesome; and perhaps, in the midst of the years we count upon, <hi type="italic">it is soon cut off, and we fly away,</hi> and do not live out half our days. <div eID="gen12113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12114" type="x-p"/> IV. They are taught by all this to stand in awe of the wrath of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who knows the power of thy anger?</hi> 1. None can perfectly comprehend it. The psalmist speaks as one afraid of God's anger, and amazed at the greatness of the power of it; who knows how far the power of God's anger can reach and how deeply it can wound? The angels that sinned knew experimentally the power of God's anger; damned sinners in hell know it; but which of us can fully comprehend or describe it? 2. Few do seriously consider it as they ought. <hi type="italic">Who knows it,</hi> so as to improve the knowledge of it? Those who make a mock at sin, and make light of Christ, surely do not know the power of God's anger. For, <hi type="italic">according to thy fear, so is thy wrath;</hi> God's wrath is equal to the apprehensions which the most thoughtful serious people have of it; let men have ever so great a dread upon them of the wrath of God, it is not greater than there is cause for and than the nature of the thing deserves. God has not in his word represented his wrath as more terrible than really it is; nay, what is felt in the other world is infinitely worse than what is feared in this world. <hi type="italic">Who among us can dwell with that devouring fire?</hi>
entries.a52bafff4848342fa29b44a913b6f101a56c2852: <div eID="gen12114" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayers for Mercy.</title> <div sID="gen12115" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> So teach <hi type="italic">us</hi> to number our days, that we may apply <hi type="italic">our</hi> hearts unto wisdom. <hi type="super">13</hi> Return, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , how long? and let it repent thee concerning thy servants. <hi type="super">14</hi> O satisfy us early with thy mercy; that we may rejoice and be glad all our days. <hi type="super">15</hi> Make us glad according to the days <hi type="italic">wherein</hi> thou hast afflicted us, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the years <hi type="italic">wherein</hi> we have seen evil. <hi type="super">16</hi> Let thy work appear unto thy servants, and thy glory unto their children. <hi type="super">17</hi> And let the beauty of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it. <div eID="gen12115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12116" type="x-p"/> These are the petitions of this prayer, grounded upon the foregoing meditations and acknowledgments. <hi type="italic">Is any afflicted? Let him</hi> learn thus to <hi type="italic">pray.</hi> Four things they are here directed to pray for:— <div eID="gen12116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12117" type="x-p"/> I. For a sanctified use of the sad dispensation they were now under. Being condemned to have our days shortened, "<hi type="italic">Lord, teach us to number our days</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.12">v. 12</reference>); Lord, give us grace duly to consider how few they are, and how little a while we have to live in this world." Note, 1. It is an excellent art rightly <hi type="italic">to number our days,</hi> so as not to be out in our calculation, as he was who counted upon many years to come when, that night, his soul was required of him. We must live under a constant apprehension of the shortness and uncertainty of life and the near approach of death and eternity. We must so number our days as to compare our work with them, and mind it accordingly with a double diligence, as those that have no time to trifle. 2. Those that would learn this arithmetic must pray for divine instruction, must go to God, and beg of him to teach them by his Spirit, to put them upon considering and to give them a good understanding. 3. We then number our days to good purpose when thereby our hearts are inclined and engaged to true wisdom, that is, to the practice of serious godliness. To be religious is to be wise; this is a thing to which it is necessary that we apply our hearts, and the matter requires and deserves a close application, to which frequent thoughts of the uncertainty of our continuance here, and the certainty of our removal hence, will very much contribute. <div eID="gen12117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12118" type="x-p"/> II. For the turning away of God's anger from them, that though the decree had gone forth, and was past revocation, there was no remedy, but they must die in the wilderness: "<hi type="italic">Yet return, O Lord!</hi> be thou reconciled to us, and <hi type="italic">let it repent thee concerning thy servants</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.13">v. 13</reference>); send us tidings of peace to comfort us again after these heavy tidings. How long must we look upon ourselves as under thy wrath, and when shall we have some token given us of our restoration to thy favour? <hi type="italic">We are thy servants, thy people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.9">Isa. lxiv. 9</reference>); when wilt thou change thy way toward us?" In answer to this prayer, and upon their profession of repentance (<reference osisRef="Num.14.39-Num.14.40">Num. xiv. 39, 40</reference>), God, in the next chapter, proceeding with the laws concerning sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Num.15.1-Num.15.31">Num. xv. 1</reference>, &c.), which was a token that it repented him concerning his servants; for, <hi type="italic">if the Lord had been pleased to kill them, he would not have shown them such things as these.</hi> <div eID="gen12118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12119" type="x-p"/> III. For comfort and joy in the returns of God's favour to them, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.14-Ps.90.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. They pray for the mercy of God; for they pretend not to plead any merit of their own. <hi type="italic">Have mercy upon us, O God!</hi> is a prayer we are all concerned to say <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> to. Let us pray for early mercy, the seasonable communications of divine mercy, that God's <hi type="italic">tender mercies may speedily prevent us, early in the morning</hi> of our days, when we are young and flourishing, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.6">v. 6</reference>. Let us pray for the true satisfaction and happiness which are to be had only in the favour and mercy of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6-Ps.4.7">Ps. iv. 6, 7</reference>. A gracious soul, if it may but be satisfied of God's lovingkindness, will be satisfied with it, abundantly satisfied, will take up with that, and will take up with nothing short of it. Two things are pleaded to enforce this petition for God's mercy:— 1. That it would be a full fountain of future joys: "<hi type="italic">O satisfy us with thy mercy,</hi> not only that we may be easy and at rest within ourselves, which we can never be while we lie under thy wrath, but that we <hi type="italic">may rejoice and be glad,</hi> not only for a time, upon the first indications of thy favour, but <hi type="italic">all our days,</hi> though we are to spend them in the wilderness." With respect to those that make God their chief joy, as their joy may be full (<reference osisRef="1John.1.4">1 John i. 4</reference>), so it may be constant, even in this vale of tears; it is their own fault if they are not glad all their days, for his mercy will furnish them with joy in tribulation and nothing can separate them from it. 2. That it would be a sufficient balance to their former griefs: "<hi type="italic">Make us glad according to the days wherein thou has afflicted us;</hi> let the days of our joy in thy favour be as many as the days of our pain for thy displeasure have been and as pleasant as those have been gloomy. <hi type="italic">Lord, thou usest to set the one over-against the other</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Eccl. vii. 14</reference>); do so in our case. Let it suffice that we have drunk so long of the cup of trembling; now put into our hands the cup of salvation." God's people reckon the returns of God's lovingkindness a sufficient recompence for all their troubles. <div eID="gen12119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12120" type="x-p"/> IV. For the progress of the work of God among them notwithstanding, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.16-Ps.90.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. 1. That he would manifest himself in carrying it on: "<hi type="italic">Let thy work appear upon thy servants;</hi> let it appear that thou hast wrought upon us, to bring us home to thyself and to fit us for thyself." God's servants cannot work for him unless he work upon them, and work in them both to will and to do; and then we may hope the operations of God's providence will be apparent for us when the operations of his grace are apparent upon us. "Let thy work appear, and in it thy glory will appear to us and those that shall come after us." In praying for God's grace God's glory must be our end; and we must therein have an eye to our children as well as to ourselves, that they also may experience God's glory appearing upon them, so as to change them into the same image, from glory to glory. Perhaps, in this prayer, they distinguish between themselves and their children, for so God distinguished in his late message to them (<reference osisRef="Num.14.31">Num. xiv. 31</reference>, <hi type="italic">Your carcases shall fall in this wilderness, but your little ones I will bring into Canaan</hi>): "Lord," say they, "let <hi type="italic">thy work appear upon us,</hi> to reform us, and bring us to a better temper, and then <hi type="italic">let thy glory appear to our children,</hi> in performing the promise to them which we have forfeited the benefit of." 2. That he would countenance and strengthen them in carrying it on, in doing their part towards it. (1.) That he would smile upon them in it: <hi type="italic">Let the beauty of the Lord our God be upon us;</hi> let it appear that God favours us. Let us have God's ordinances kept up among us and the tokens of God's presence with his ordinances; so some. We may apply this petition both to our sanctification and to our consolation. Holiness is <hi type="italic">the beauty of the Lord our God;</hi> let that be upon us in all we say and do; let the grace of God in us, and the light of our good works, make our faces to shine (that is the comeliness God puts upon us, and those are comely indeed who are so beautified), and then let divine consolations put gladness into our hearts, and a lustre upon our countenances, and that also will be the beauty of the Lord upon us, as our God. (2.) That he would prosper them in it: <hi type="italic">Establish thou the work of our hands upon us.</hi> God's working upon us (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.16">v. 16</reference>) does not discharge us from using our utmost endeavours in serving him and working out our salvation. But, when we have done all, we must wait upon God for the success, and beg of him to <hi type="italic">prosper our handy works,</hi> to give us to compass what we aim at for his glory. We are so unworthy of divine assistance, and yet so utterly insufficient to bring any thing to pass without it, that we have need to be earnest for it and to repeat the request: <hi type="italic">Yea, the work of our hands, establish thou it,</hi> and, in order to that, establish us in it.  <chapter eID="Ps.90"/> <div eID="gen12120" type="x-p"/>

entries.3457db4da95133a7ca23ce08db1ad8510224b70c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6554"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 90</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.90.1-Ps.90.17">Psa 90:1-17</reference>. Contrasting man's frailty with God's eternity, the writer mourns over it as the punishment of sin, and prays for a return of the divine favor. A Prayer [mainly such] of Moses the man of God--(<reference osisRef="Deut.33.1">De 33:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.14.6">Jos 14:6</reference>); as such he wrote this (see on <reference osisRef="Ps.18.1">Psa 18:1</reference>, title, and <reference osisRef="Ps.36.1">Psa 36:1</reference>, title).</title> <div sID="gen10046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6554"/><hi type="bold">1. dwelling-place--</hi>home (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.16">Eze 11:16</reference>), as a refuge (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.27">De 33:27</reference>). <div eID="gen10046" type="x-p"/>
entries.a54fff0f1e4f01401f6411374e7d16d7248bba84: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6555"/><div sID="gen10047" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6555"/><hi type="bold">2. brought forth [and] formed--</hi>both express the idea of production by birth. <div eID="gen10047" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb1f84abdaddff3c4bcf3002fdaa2d6c5d033697: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6556"/><div sID="gen10048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6556"/><hi type="bold">3. to destruction--</hi>literally, "even to dust" (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.19">Ge 3:19</reference>), which is partly quoted in the last clause. <div eID="gen10048" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e1239a47d5980de706004ea8c167f925a439f11: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6557"/><div sID="gen10049" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6557"/>4. Even were our days now a thousand years, as Adam's, our life would be but a moment in God's sight (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.8">2Pe 3:8</reference>).<div eID="gen10049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a watch--</hi>or, third part of a night (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.14.24">Ex 14:24</reference>). <div eID="gen10050" type="x-p"/>
entries.964ffc4ab41d2103345fa9040465f95e98d251e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6558"/><div sID="gen10051" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6558"/>5-6. Life is like grass, which, though changing under the influence of the night's dew, and flourishing in the morning, is soon cut down and withereth (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.15">Psa 103:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.24">1Pe 1:24</reference>). <div eID="gen10051" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a51157e272a8e71670858ef46a552edca2a657a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6559"/><div sID="gen10052" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6559"/><hi type="bold">7-8. For--</hi>A reason, this is the infliction of God's wrath.<div eID="gen10052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">troubled--</hi>literally, "confounded by terror" (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.5">Psa 2:5</reference>). Death is by sin (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.12">Ro 5:12</reference>). Though "secret," the light of God's countenance, as a candle, will bring sin to view (<reference osisRef="Prov.20.27">Pr 20:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">1Co 4:5</reference>). <div eID="gen10053" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c44b75e0b78c08b733adc4759fe3d77b2fa9789: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6560"/><div sID="gen10054" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6560"/><hi type="bold">9. are passed--</hi>literally, "turn," as to depart (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.4">Jr 6:4</reference>).<div eID="gen10054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spend--</hi>literally, "consume."<div eID="gen10055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a tale--</hi>literally, "a thought," or, "a sigh" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.2.10">Eze 2:10</reference>). <div eID="gen10056" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d4139ad823d8dfce4682074f0f22aff3d29a6ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6561"/><div sID="gen10057" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6561"/>10. Moses' life was an exception (<reference osisRef="Deut.34.7">De 34:7</reference>).<div eID="gen10057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it is ... cut off--</hi>or, "driven," as is said of the quails in using the same word (<reference osisRef="Num.11.31">Nu 11:31</reference>). In view of this certain and speedy end, life is full of sorrow. <div eID="gen10058" type="x-p"/>
entries.b828941387713ee08ca994169bdb76880d278626: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6562"/><div sID="gen10059" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6562"/>11. The whole verse may be read as a question implying the negative, "No one knows what Thy anger can do, and what Thy wrath is, estimated by a true piety." <div eID="gen10059" type="x-p"/>
entries.448904db66b65cb26c452c206dc9a78254132a58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6563"/><div sID="gen10060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6563"/>12. This he prays we may know or understand, so as properly to number or appreciate the shortness of our days, that we may be wise. <div eID="gen10060" type="x-p"/>
entries.8087874bc3df3a6417b9bf731b5968836a0f7b53: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6564"/><div sID="gen10061" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6564"/>13. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.13.2">Psa 13:2</reference>).<div eID="gen10061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let it repent--</hi>a strong figure, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.32.12">Ex 32:12</reference>, imploring a change in His dealings. <div eID="gen10062" type="x-p"/>
entries.271d8cff4641b19cef9a070960776091875ca545: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6565"/><div sID="gen10063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6565"/><hi type="bold">14. early--</hi>promptly. <div eID="gen10063" type="x-p"/>
entries.be8b55706342391f524f32d3326e404aabfbcda1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6566"/><div sID="gen10064" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6566"/>15. As have been our sorrows, so let our joys be great and long. <div eID="gen10064" type="x-p"/>
entries.faf8281d72b8a8cad3aa01df578f54c19c627a2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6567"/><div sID="gen10065" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6567"/><hi type="bold">16. thy work--</hi>or, providential acts.<div eID="gen10065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy glory--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">Psa 8:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.3">45:3</reference>), the honor accruing from Thy work of mercy to us. <div eID="gen10066" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a28174bdbea25c65b1e4f0d80cb8b39214a5e21: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6568"/><div sID="gen10067" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6568"/><hi type="bold">17. let the beauty--</hi>or sum of His gracious acts, in their harmony, be illustrated in us, and favor our enterprise. <chapter eID="Ps.90"/>

entries.95e6b217701c56fc8e21afaa8ccf5a033cba174c: <div eID="gen21590" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21591" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21592" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21592" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21591" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21593" type="x-p"/> The eternity of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.90.1">Psa 90:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.90.2">Psa 90:2</reference>; the frailty of the state of man, <reference osisRef="Psa.90.3-Psa.90.9">Psa 90:3-9</reference>; the general limits of human life, <reference osisRef="Psa.90.10">Psa 90:10</reference>; the danger of displeasing God, <reference osisRef="Psa.90.11">Psa 90:11</reference>; the necessity of considering the shortness of life, and of regaining the favor of the Almighty, <reference osisRef="Psa.90.12">Psa 90:12</reference>; earnest prayer for the restoration of Israel, <reference osisRef="Psa.90.13-Psa.90.17">Psa 90:13-17</reference>. <div eID="gen21593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21594" type="x-p"/> The title of this Psalm is, A Prayer of Moses the man of God. The Chaldee has, "A prayer which Moses the prophet of the Lord prayed when the people of Israel had sinned in the wilderness." All the Versions ascribe it to Moses; but that it could not be of Moses the lawgiver is evident from this consideration, that the age of man was not then seventy or eighty years, which is here stated to be its almost universal limit, for Joshua lived one hundred and ten years, and Moses himself one hundred and twenty; Miriam his sister, one hundred and thirty; Aaron his brother, one hundred and twenty-three; Caleb, four-score and five years; and their contemporaries lived in the same proportion. See the note on <reference osisRef="Psa.90.4">Psa 90:4</reference> (note). Therefore the Psalm cannot at all refer to such ancient times. If the title be at all authentic, it must refer to some other person of that name; and indeed איש אלהים ish Elohim, a man of God, a divinely inspired man, agrees to the times of the prophets, who were thus denominated. The Psalm was doubtless composed during or after the captivity; and most probably on their return, when they were engaged in rebuilding the temple; and this, as Dr. Kennicott conjectures, may be the work of their hands, which they pray God to bless and prosper. <div eID="gen21594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21595" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21596" type="x-p"/> Lord, thou hast been our dwellingplace - מעון maon; but instead of this several MSS. have מעוז maoz, "place of defense," or "refuge," which is the reading of the Vulgate, Septuagint, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon. Ever since thy covenant with Abraham thou hast been the Resting-place, Refuge, and Defence of thy people Israel. Thy mercy has been lengthened out from generation to generation.
entries.4bd7da5660a51e722703deec438969063df3ad7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21597" type="x-p"/> Before the mountains were brought forth - The mountains and hills appear to have been everlasting; but as they were brought forth out of the womb of eternity, there was a time when they were not: but Thou hast been ab aeternitate a parte ante, ad aeternitatem a parte post; fram the eternity that is past, before time began; to the eternity that is after, when time shall have an end. This is the highest description of the eternity of God to which human language can reach.
entries.e2d0bc2a34e84c77d9572f1d7045de4bb0b2f874: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21598" type="x-p"/> Thou turnest man to destruction - Literally, Thou shalt turn dying man, אנוש enosh, to the small dust, דכא dacca but thou wilt say, Return, ye children of Adam. This appears to be a clear and strong promise of the resurrection of the human body, after it has long slept, mingled with the dust of the earth.
entries.a003da1605cb0e483b6c1f9eff2f5342c4e0b35c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21599" type="x-p"/> For a thousand years in thy sight - As if he had said, Though the resurrection of the body may be a thousand (or any indefinite number of) years distant; yet, when these are past, they are but as yesterday, or a single thatch of the night. They pass through the mind in a moment, and appear no longer in their duration than the time required by the mind to reflect them by thought. But, short as they appear to the eye of the mind, they are nothing when compared with the eternity of God! The author probably has in view also that economy of Divine justice and providence by which the life of man has been shortened from one thousand years to threescore years and ten, or fourscore.
entries.fe7c20371f85982a7065f840588d9518d7824de0: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21600" type="x-p"/> Thou carriest them away as with a flood - Life is compared to a stream, ever gliding away; but sometimes it is as a mighty torrent, when by reason of plague, famine, or war, thousands are swept away daily. In particular cases it is a rapid stream, when the young are suddenly carried off by consumptions, fevers, etc.; this is the flower that flourisheth in the morning, and in the evening is cut down and withered. The whole of life is like a sleep or as a dream. The eternal world is real; all here is either shadowy or representative. On the whole, life is represented as a stream; youth, as morning; decline of life, or old age, as evening, death, as sleep; and the resurrection as the return of the flowers in spring. All these images appear in these curious and striking verses, <reference osisRef="Psa.90.3-Psa.90.6">Psa 90:3-6</reference>.
entries.1d370a6bc26131caaa43b24700367569c57570a6: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21601" type="x-p"/> We are consumed by thine anger - Death had not entered into the world, if men had not fallen from God. <div eID="gen21601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21602" type="x-p"/> By thy wrath are we troubled - Pain, disease, and sickness are so many proofs of our defection from original rectitude. The anger and wrath of God are moved against all sinners. Even in protracted life we consume away, and only seem to live in order to die. "Our wasting lives grow shorter still,As days and months increase; <div eID="gen21602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21603" type="x-p"/> And every beating pulse we tellLeaves but the number less."
entries.e12f76ffdfbd26dac445d516c29b23b1bd05f022: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21604" type="x-p"/> Thou hast set our iniquities before thee - Every one of our transgressions is set before thee; noted and minuted down in thy awful register! <div eID="gen21604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21605" type="x-p"/> Our secret sins - Those committed in darkness and privacy are easily discovered by thee, being shown by the splendours of thy face shining upon them. Thus we light a candle, and bring it into a dark place to discover its contents. O, what can be hidden from the allseeing eye of God? Darkness is no darkness to him; wherever he comes there is a profusion of light - for God is light!
entries.3941af7d02594e46e8571fb985b9f877280da165: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21606" type="x-p"/> We spend our years as a tale - The Vulgate has: Anni nostri sicut aranea meditabuntur; "Our years pass away like those of the spider." Our plans and operations are like the spider's web; life is as frail, and the thread of it as brittle, as one of those that constitute the well-wrought and curious, but fragile, habitation of that insect. All the Versions have the word spider; but it neither appears in the Hebrew, nor in any of its MSS. which have been collated. <div eID="gen21606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21607" type="x-p"/> My old Psalter has a curious paraphrase here: "Als the iran (spider) makes vayne webs for to take flese (flies) with gile, swa our yeres ere ockupide in ydel and swikel castes about erthly thynges; and passes with outen frute of gude werks, and waste in ydel thynkyns." This is too true a picture of most lives. <div eID="gen21607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21608" type="x-p"/> But the Hebrew is different from all the Versions. "We consume our years (כמו הגה kemo hegeh) like a groan." We live a dying, whining, complaining life, and at last a groan is its termination! How amazingly expressive!
entries.652b88c3bc3872b0a61420fde41df0125fa34255: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21609" type="x-p"/> Threescore years and ten - See the note on the title of this Psalm 90 (note). This Psalm could not have been written by Moses, because the term of human life was much more extended when he flourished than eighty years at the most. Even in David's time many lived one hundred years, and the author of Ecclesiasticus, who lived after the captivity, fixed this term at one hundred years at the most (Sirach 18:9); but this was merely a general average, for even in our country we have many who exceed a hundred years. <div eID="gen21609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21610" type="x-p"/> Yet is their strength labor and sorrow - This refers to the infirmities of old age, which, to those well advanced in life, produce labor and sorrow. <div eID="gen21610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21611" type="x-p"/> It is soon cut of - It - the body, is soon cut off. <div eID="gen21611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21612" type="x-p"/> And we fly away - The immortal spirit wings its way into the eternal world.
entries.cc5e27912c4cc0b06344d09c9ce49507a93a0257: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21613" type="x-p"/> Who knoweth the power of thine angers - The afflictions of this life are not to be compared to the miseries which await them who live and die without being reconciled to God, and saved from their sins.
entries.a7c0786420148a16abc82fcbe2280a2d9f0845dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21614" type="x-p"/> So teach us to number our days - Let us deeply consider our own frailty, and the shortness and uncertainty of life, that we may live for eternity, acquaint ourselves with thee and be at peace; that we may die in thy favor and live and reign with thee eternally.
entries.e89fdc762b55ddc50bcaa425e02206dd6015675c: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen21614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21615" type="x-p"/> Return, O Lord, how long? - Wilt thou continue angry with us for ever? <div eID="gen21615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21616" type="x-p"/> Let it repent thee - הנחם hinnachem, be comforted, rejoice over them to do them good. Be glorified rather in our salvation than in our destruction.
entries.ae9f78ca126f1029eabee5d4e6102de8cecd6b9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen21616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21617" type="x-p"/> O satisfy us early - Let us have thy mercy soon, (literally, in the morning). Let it now shine upon us, and it shall seem as the morning of our days, and we shall exult in thee all the days of our life.
entries.b272ecc1a2a644a3e0526f0a0c12c589e438f55a: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen21617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21618" type="x-p"/> Make us glad according to the days - Let thy people have as many years of prosperity as they have had of adversity. We have now suffered seventy years of a most distressful captivity.
entries.e283b472815943794740ae720df8528022e832c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen21618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21619" type="x-p"/> Let thy work appear unto thy servants - That thou art working for us we know; but O, let thy work appear! Let us now see, in our deliverance, that thy thoughts towards us were mercy and love. <div eID="gen21619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21620" type="x-p"/> And thy Glory - Thy pure worship be established among our children for ever.
entries.505005133ab10fd165246ddf0c69f6507d015848: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen21620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21621" type="x-p"/> And let the beauty of the Lord - Let us have thy presence, blessing, and approbation, as our fathers had. <div eID="gen21621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21622" type="x-p"/> Establish thou the work of our hands - This is supposed, we have already seen, to relate to their rebuilding the temple, which the surrounding heathens and Samaritans wished to hinder. We have begun, do not let them demolish our work; let the top-stone be brought on with shouting, Grace, grace unto it. <div eID="gen21622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21623" type="x-p"/> Yea, the work of our hands - This repetition is wanting in three of Kennicott's MSS., in the Targum, in the Septuagint, and in the Ethiopic. If the repetition be genuine, it may be considered as marking great earnestness; and this earnestness was to get the temple of God rebuilt, and his pure worship restored. The pious Jews had this more at heart than their own restoration; it was their highest grief that the temple was destroyed and God's ordinances suspended; that his enemies insulted them, and blasphemed the worthy name by which they were called. Every truly pious man feels more for God's glory than his own temporal felicity, and rejoices more in the prosperity of God's work than in the increase of his own worldly goods.  <chapter eID="Ps.90"/> <div eID="gen21623" type="x-p"/>

entries.1b6b74e22d47de48716b182ce3b1a34e1be795f6: <div eID="gen9898" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Taking Refuge in the loving-kindness of the Eternal One under the Wrathful Judgment of Death</title> <div sID="gen9899" type="x-p"/> The Fourth Book of the Psalms, corresponding to the ספר במדבר of the Pentateuch, begins with a <hi type="italic">Prayer of Moses the man of God</hi>, which comes out of the midst of the dying off of the older generation during the march through the wilderness. To the name, which could not be allowed to remain so bald, because next to Abraham he is the greatest man known to the Old Testament history of redemption, is added the title of honour אישׁ האלהים (as in <reference osisRef="Deut.33.1">Deu 33:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.14.6">Jos 14:6</reference>), an ancient name of the prophets which expresses the close relationship of fellowship with God, just as “servant of Jahve” expresses the relationship of service, in accordance with the special office and in relation to the history of redemption, into which Jahve has taken the man and into which he himself has entered. There is scarcely any written memorial of antiquity which so brilliantly justifies the testimony of tradition concerning its origin as does this Psalm, which may have been preserved in some one or other of the older works, perhaps the “Book of Jashar” (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.13">Jos 10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.18">2Sa 1:18</reference>), until the time of the final redaction of the Psalter. Not alone with respect to its contents, but also with reference to the form of its language, it is perfectly suitable to Moses. Even Hitzig can bring nothing of importance against this view, for the objection that the author in v. 1 glances back upon past generations, whilst Israel was only born in the time of Moses, is removed by the consideration that the existence of Israel reaches back into the patriarchal times; and there is as little truth in the assertion that the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> שׂבּענוּ in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.14">Psa 90:14</reference> instead of the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> brings the Psalm down into very late times, as in the idea that the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. והאבדתּ in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.12">Psa 143:12</reference> instead of the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> carries this <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1-Ps.143.12">Psa 143:1-12</reference> back into very early times. These trifling points dwindle down to nothing in comparison with the fact that Psalms 90 bears within itself distinct traces of the same origin as the song האזינו (Deut. 32), the blessing of Moses (Deut. 33), the discourses in Deuteronomy, and in general the directly Mosaic portions of the Pentateuch. The Book of the Covenant, together with the Decalogue (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.1">Exo 19:1</reference>) and Deuteronomy (with the exception of its supplement), are regarded by us, on very good grounds, as the largest originally Mosaic constituent parts of the Pentateuch. The Book of Deuteronomy is תּורת משׁה in a pre-eminent sense.
entries.a185280f2cc125966c62af352b0f681690229ad5: <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1-Ps.90.4">Psa 90:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen9899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9900" type="x-p"/> The poet begins with the confession that the Lord has proved Himself to His own, in all periods of human history, as that which He was before the world was and will be for evermore. God is designedly appealed to by the name אדני, which frequently occurs in the mouth of Moses in the middle books of the Pentateuch, and also in the Song at the Sea, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.17">Exo 15:17</reference> and in Deu 3:24. He is so named here as the Lord ruling over human history with an exaltation ever the same. Human history runs on in דּר ודר, so that one period (περίοδος) with the men living contemporaneous with it goes and another comes; the expression is deuteronomic (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.7">Deu 32:7</reference>). Such a course of generations lies behind the poet; and in them all the Lord has been מעון to His church, out of the heart of which the poet discourses. This expression too is Deuteronomic (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.27">Deu 33:27</reference>). מעון signifies a habitation, dwelling-place (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.26.8">Psa 26:8</reference>), more especially God’s heavenly and earthly dwelling-place, then the dwelling-place which God Himself is to His saints, inasmuch as He takes up to Himself, conceals and protects, those who flee to Him from the wicked one and from evil, and turn in to Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.3">Psa 71:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.9">Psa 91:9</reference>). In order to express <hi type="italic">fuisti</hi> היית was indispensable; but just as <hi type="italic">fuisti</hi> comes from <hi type="italic">fuo</hi>, φύω, היה (הוה) signifies not a closed, shut up being, but a being that discloses itself, consequently it is <hi type="italic">fuisti</hi> in the sense of <hi type="italic">te exhibuisti</hi>. This historical self-manifestation of god is based upon the fact that He is אל, i.e., might absolutely, or the absolutely Mighty One; and He was this, as <reference osisRef="Ps.90.2">Psa 90:2</reference> says, even before the beginning of the history of the present world, and will be in the distant ages of the future as of the past. The foundation of this world’s history is the creation. The combination ארץ ותבל shows that this is intended to be taken as the object. ותּחולל (with <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> beside the <hi type="italic">e4</hi> of the final syllable, which is deprived of its accent, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.18.20">Psa 18:20</reference>) is the language of address (Rashi): that which is created is in a certain sense born from God (ילּד), and He brings it forth out of Himself; and this is here expressed by חולל (as in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.18">Deu 32:18</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.51.2">Isa 51:2</reference>), creation being compared to travail which takes place amidst pains (<hi type="italic">Psychology</hi>, S. 114; tr. p. 137). If, after the example of the lxx and Targum, one reads as passive ותּחולל (Böttcher, Olshausen, Hitzig) from the <hi type="italic">Pulal</hi> חולל, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.24">Pro 8:24</reference>, - and this commends itself, since the pre-existence of God can be better dated back beyond facts than beyond the acts of God Himself, - then the conception remains essentially the same, since the Eternal and Absolute One is still to be thought of as מחולל. The fact that the mountains are mentioned first of all, harmonizes with Deu 33:15. The <hi type="italic">modus consecutivus</hi> is intended to say: before the mountains were brought forth and Thou wast in labour therewith.... The forming of the mountains consequently coincides with the creation of the earth, which is here as a body or mass called ארץ, and as a continent with the relief of mountains and lowlands is called תבל (cf. תבל ארץ, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.31">Pro 8:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.37.12">Job 37:12</reference>). To the double clause with טרם <hi type="italic">seq. praet.</hi> (cf. on the other hand <hi type="italic">seq.</hi> <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">Deu 31:21</reference>) is appended וּמעולם as a second definition of time: before the creation of the world, and from eternity to eternity. The Lord was God before the world was - that is the first assertion of <reference osisRef="Ps.90.2">Psa 90:2</reference>; His divine existence reaches out of the unlimited past into the unlimited future - this is the second. אל is not vocative, which it sometimes, though rarely, is in the Psalms; it is a predicate, as e.g., in Deu 3:24. <div eID="gen9900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9901" type="x-p"/> This is also to be seen from <reference osisRef="Ps.90.3">Psa 90:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.4">Psa 90:4</reference>, when <reference osisRef="Ps.90.3">Psa 90:3</reference> now more definitely affirms the omnipotence of God, and <reference osisRef="Ps.90.4">Psa 90:4</reference> the supra-temporality of God or the omnipresence of God in time. The lxx misses the meaning when it brings over אל from <reference osisRef="Ps.90.2">Psa 90:2</reference>, and reads אל־תּשׁב. The shorter future form תּשׁב for תּשׁיב stands poetically instead of the longer, as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Psa 11:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.26.9">Psa 26:9</reference>; cf. the same thing in the <hi type="italic">inf. constr.</hi> in <reference osisRef="Deut.26.12">Deu 26:12</reference>, and both instances together in Deu 32:8. The poet intentionally calls the generation that is dying away אנושׁ, which denotes man from the side of his frailty or perishableness; and the new generation בּני־אדם, with which is combined the idea of entrance upon life. It is clear that השׁיב עד־דּכּא is intended to be understood according to <reference osisRef="Gen.3.19">Gen 3:19</reference>; but it is a question whether דּכּא is conceived of as an adjective (with mutable <hi type="italic">aa</hi>), as in <reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">Psa 34:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa 57:15</reference> : Thou puttest men back into the condition of crushed ones (cf. on the construction Num 24:24), or whether as a neutral feminine from דּך (= דּכּה): Thou changest them into that which is crushed = dust, or whether as an abstract substantive like דּכּה, or according to another reading (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.127.2">Psa 127:2</reference>) דּכּא, in <reference osisRef="Deut.23.2">Deu 23:2</reference> : to crushing. This last is the simplest way of taking it, but it comes to one and the same thing with the second, since דּכּא signifies crushing in the neuter sense. A <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. follows. The fact that God causes one generation to die off has as its consequence that He calls another into being (cf. the Arabic epithet of God <hi type="italic">el - mu‛ı̂d</hi> = המשׁיב, the Resuscitator). Hofmann and Hitzig take תּשׁב as imperfect on account of the following ותּאמר: Thou didst decree mortality for men; but the <hi type="italic">fut. consec. </hi>frequently only expresses the sequence of the thoughts or the connection of the matter, e.g., after a future that refers to that which is constantly taking place, Job 14:10. God causes men to die without letting them die out; for - so it continues in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.4">Psa 90:4</reference> - a thousand years is to Him a very short period, not to be at all taken into account. What now is the connection between that which confirms and that which is confirmed here? It is not so much <reference osisRef="Ps.90.3">Psa 90:3</reference> that is confirmed as <reference osisRef="Ps.90.2">Psa 90:2</reference>, to which the former serves for explanation, viz., this, that God as the Almighty (אל), in the midst of this change of generations, which is His work, remains Himself eternally the same. This ever the same, absolute existence has its ground herein, that time, although God fills it up with His working, is no limitation to Him. A thousand years, which would make any man who might live through them weary of life, are to Him like a vanishing point. The proposition, as 2Pe 3:8 shows, is also true when reversed: “One day is with the Lord as a thousand years.” He is however exalted above all time, inasmuch as the longest period appears to Him very short, and in the shortest period the greatest work can be executed by Him. The standpoint of the first comparison, <hi type="italic">“as yesterday,”</hi> is taken towards the end of the thousand of years. A whole millennium appears to God, when He glances over it, just as the yesterday does to us when (כּי) it is passing by (יעבר), and we, standing on the border of the opening day, look back upon the day that is gone. The second comparison is an advance upon the first, and an advance also in form, from the fact that the <hi type="italic">Caph similitudinis</hi> is wanting: a thousand years are to God a watch in the night. אשׁמוּרה is a night-watch, of which the Israelites reckoned three, viz., the first, the middle, and the morning watch (vid., Winer’s <hi type="italic">Realwörterbuch</hi> s. v. <hi type="italic">Nachtwache</hi>). It is certainly not without design that the poet says אשׁמוּרה בלּילה instead of אשׁמרת הלּילה. The night-time is the time for sleep; a watch in the night is one that is slept away, or at any rate passed in a sort of half-sleep. A day that is past, as we stand on the end of it, still produces upon us the impression of a course of time by reason of the events which we can recall; but a night passed in sleep, and now even a fragment of the night, is devoid of all trace to us, and is therefore as it were timeless. Thus is it to God with a thousand years: they do not last long to Him; they do not affect Him; at the close of them, as at the beginning, He is the Absolute One (אל). Time is as nothing to Him, the Eternal One. The changes of time are to Him no barrier restraining the realization of His counsel - a truth which has a terrible and a consolatory side. The poet dwells upon the fear which it produces.
entries.2461fce801239e8bf5a452e43ae82528a3269809: <reference osisRef="Ps.90.5-Ps.90.8">Psa 90:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen9901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9902" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.90.5-Ps.90.6">Psa 90:5-6</reference> tell us how great is the distance between men and this eternal selfsameness of God. The suffix of זרמתּם, referred to the thousand years, produces a synallage (since שׁנה is feminine), which is to be avoided whenever it is possible to do so; the reference to בני־אדם, as being the principal object pointed to in what has gone before, is the more natural, to say the very least. In connection with both ways of applying it, זרם does not signify: to cause to rattle down like sudden heavy showers of rain; for the figure that God makes years, or that He makes men (Hitzig: the germs of their coming into being), to rain down from above, is fanciful and strange. זרם may also mean to sweep or wash away as with heavy rains, <hi type="italic">abripere instar nimbi</hi>, as the old expositors take it. So too Luther at one time: <hi type="italic">Du reyssest sie dahyn</hi> (Thou carriest them away), for which he substituted later: <hi type="italic">Du lessest sie dahin faren wie einen Strom</hi> (Thou causest them to pass away as a river); but זרם always signifies rain pouring down from above. As a sudden and heavy shower of rain, becoming a flood, washes everything away, so God’s omnipotence sweeps men away. There is now no transition to another alien figure when the poet continues: שׁנה יהיוּ. What is meant is the sleep of death, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.6">Psa 76:6</reference>, שׁנת עולם, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.39">Jer 51:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.57">Jer 51:57</reference>, cf. ישׁן Psa 13:4. He whom a flood carries away is actually brought into a state of unconsciousness, he goes entirely to sleep, i.e., he dies. <div eID="gen9902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9903" type="x-p"/> From this point the poet certainly does pass on to another figure. The one generation is carried away as by a flood in the night season, and in the morning another grows up. Men are the subject of יחלף, as of יהיוּ. The collective singular alternates with the plural, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.3">Psa 90:3</reference> the collective אנושׁ alternates with בני־אדם. The two members of <reference osisRef="Ps.90.5">Psa 90:5</reference> stand in contrast. The poet describes the succession of the generations. One generation perishes as it were in a flood, and another grows up, and this also passes on to the same fate. The meaning in both verses of the חלף, which has been for the most part, after the lxx, Vulgate, and Luther, erroneously taken to be <hi type="italic">praeterire = interire</hi>, is determined in accordance with this idea. The general signification of this verb, which corresponds to the Arabic <hi type="italic">chlf</hi>, is “to follow or move after, to go into the place of another, and in general, of passing over from one place or state into another.” Accordingly the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> signifies to put into a new condition, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.27">Psa 102:27</reference>, to set a new thing on the place of an old one, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.9">Isa 9:9</reference> [10], to gain new strength, to take fresh courage, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Isa 40:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.1">Isa 41:1</reference>; and of plants: to send forth new shoots, <reference osisRef="Job.14.7">Job 14:7</reference>; consequently the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, which frequently furnishes the perfect for the future <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> (Ew. §127, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, and Hitzig on this passage), of plants signifies: to gain new shoots, not: to sprout (Targum, Syriac), but to sprout again or afresh, <hi type="italic">regerminare</hi>; cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">chilf</hi>, an aftergrowth, new wood. Perishing humanity renews its youth in ever new generations. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.90.6">Psa 90:6</reference></hi> again takes up this thought: in the morning it grows up and shoots afresh, viz., the grass to which men are likened (a figure appropriated by Isa. 40), in the evening it is cut down and it dries up. Others translate מולל to wither (root מל, properly to be long and lax, to allow to hang down long, cf. אמלל, אמל with Arab. <hi type="italic">'ml</hi>, to hope, i.e., to look forth into the distance); but (1) this <hi type="italic">Pilel</hi> of מוּל or <hi type="italic">Poēl</hi> of מלל is not favourable to this intransitive way of taking it; (2) the reflexive in <reference osisRef="Ps.58.8">Psa 58:8</reference> proves that מלל signifies to cut off in the front or above, after which perhaps even <reference osisRef="Ps.37.2">Psa 37:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.14.2">Job 14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.16">Job 18:16</reference>, by comparison with <reference osisRef="Job.24.24">Job 24:24</reference>, are to be explained. In the last passage it runs: <hi type="italic">as the top of the stalk</hi> they are cut off (<hi type="italic">fut. Niph</hi>. of מלל). Such a cut or plucked ear of corn is called in <reference osisRef="Deut.23.25">Deu 23:25</reference> מלילה, a Deuteronomic hapaxlegomenon which favours our way of taking the ימולל (with a most general subject = ימולל). Thus, too, ויבשׁ is better attached to what precedes: the cut grass becomes parched hay. Just such an alternation of morning springing froth and evening drying up is the alternation of the generations of men. <div eID="gen9903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9904" type="x-p"/> The poet substantiates this in Psa 90:7. from the experience of those amongst whom he comprehended himself in the לנוּ of <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">Psa 90:1</reference>, Hengstenberg takes <reference osisRef="Ps.90.7">Psa 90:7</reference> to be a statement of the cause of the transitoriness set forth: its cause is the wrath of God; but the poet does not begin כי באפך but כי כלינו. The chief emphasis therefore lies upon the perishing, and כי is not argumentative but explicative. If the subject of כלינוּ were men in general (Olshausen), then it would be elucidating <hi type="italic">idem per idem</hi>. But, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">Psa 90:1</reference>, those who speak here are those whose refuge the Eternal One is. The poet therefore speaks in the name of the church, and confirms the lot of men from that which his people have experienced even down to the present time. Israel is able out of its own experience to corroborate what all men pass through; it has to pass through the very same experience as a special decree of God’s wrath on account of its sins. Therefore in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.7-Ps.90.8">Psa 90:7-8</reference> we stand altogether upon historical ground. The testimony of the inscription is here verified in the contents of the Psalm. The older generation that came out of Egypt fell a prey to the sentence of punishment, that they should gradually die off during the forty years’ journey through the desert; and even Moses and Aaron, Joshua and Caleb only excepted, were included in this punishment on special grounds, Num 14:26., <reference osisRef="Deut.1.34">Deu 1:34</reference>-39. This it is over which Moses here laments. God’s wrath is here called אף and חמה; just as the Book of Deuteronomy (in distinction from the other books of the Pentateuch) is fond of combining these two synonyms (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.19">Deu 9:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.29.22">Deu 29:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.27">Deu 29:27</reference>, cf. Gen 27:44.). The breaking forth of the infinitely great opposition of the holy nature of God against sin has swept away the church in the person of its members, even down to the present moment; נבהל as in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.29">Psa 104:29</reference>, cf. בּחלה, Lev 26:16. It is the consequence of their sins. עון signifies sin as the perversion of the right standing and conduct; עלוּם, that which is veiled in distinction from manifest sins, is the sum-total of hidden moral, and that sinful, conduct. There is no necessity to regard עלמנוּ as a defective plural; עלמים signifies youth (from a radically distinct word, עלם); secret sins would therefore be called עלמות according to Psa 19:13. God sets transgressions before Him when, because the measure is full and forgiveness is inadmissible, He makes them an object of punishment. שׁתּ (<hi type="italic">Kerî</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.8.7">Psa 8:7</reference> : שׁתּה, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.6.4">Psa 6:4</reference> ואתּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.6">Psa 74:6</reference> ועתּ) has the accent upon the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> before an initial guttural. The parallel to לנגדּך is למאור פּניך. עור is light, and מאור is either a body of light, as the sun and moon, or, as in this passage, the circle of light which the light forms. The countenance of God (פני ה) is God’s nature in its inclination towards the world, and מאור פני ה is the doxa of His nature that is turned towards the world, which penetrates everything that is conformed to God as a gracious light (Num 6:25), and makes manifest to the bottom everything that is opposed to God and consumes it as a wrathful fire.
entries.9163448d133351330b080c2975bc779b26b5f1f3: <reference osisRef="Ps.90.9-Ps.90.12">Psa 90:9-12</reference> <div eID="gen9904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9905" type="x-p"/> After the transitoriness of men has now been confirmed in Psa 90:6. out of the special experience of Israel, the fact that this particular experience has its ground in a divine decree of wrath is more definitely confirmed from the facts of this experience, which, as Psa 90:11. complain, unfortunately have done so little to urge them on to the fear of God, which is the condition and the beginning of wisdom. In <reference osisRef="Ps.90.9">Psa 90:9</reference> we distinctly hear the Israel of the desert speaking. That was a generation that fell a prey to the wrath of God (דּור עברתו, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.29">Jer 7:29</reference>). עברה is wrath that passes over, breaks through the bounds of subjectivity. All their days (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.103.15">Psa 103:15</reference>) are passed away (פּנה, to turn one’s self, to turn, e.g., <reference osisRef="Deut.1.24">Deu 1:24</reference>) in such wrath, i.e., thoroughly pervaded by it. They have spent their years like a sound (כּמו־הגה), which has hardly gone forth before it has passed away, leaving no trace behind it; the noun signifies a gentle dull sound, whether a murmur (<reference osisRef="Job.37.2">Job 37:2</reference>) or a groan (<reference osisRef="Ezek.2.10">Eze 2:10</reference>). With בּהם in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.10">Psa 90:10</reference> the sum is stated: there are comprehended therein seventy years; they include, run up to so many. Hitzig renders: the days wherein (בהם) our years consist are seventy years; but שׁנותינו side by side with ימי must be regarded as its more minute genitival definition, and the accentuation cannot be objected to. Beside the plural שׁנים the poetic plural שׁנות appears here, and it also occurs in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.7">Deu 32:7</reference> (and nowhere else in the Pentateuch).
