That of which the sum is to be stated stands first of all as a <hi type="italic">casus absol</hi>. Luther’s rendering: <hi type="italic">Siebenzig Jar, wens hoch kompt so sinds achtzig </hi>(seventy years, or at the furthest eighty years), as Symmachus also meant by his ἐν παραδόξῳ (in Chrysostom), is confirmed by the Talmudic הגיע לגבורות, “to attain to extreme old age” (<hi type="italic">B. Moëd</hi> <hi type="italic">katan</hi>, 28 <hi type="italic">a</hi>), and rightly approved of by Hitzig and Olshausen. גבוּרת signifies in <reference osisRef="Ps.71.16">Psa 71:16</reference> full strength, here full measure. Seventy, or at most eighty years, were the average sum of the extreme term of life to which the generation dying out in the wilderness attained. ורהבּם the lxx renders τὸ πλεῖον αὐτῶν, but רהבּם is not equivalent to רבּם. The verb רהב signifies to behave violently, e.g., of importunate entreaty, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.3">Pro 6:3</reference>, of insolent treatment, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.5">Isa 3:5</reference>, whence רהב (here רהב), violence, impetuosity, and more especially a boastful vaunting appearance or coming forward, <reference osisRef="Job.9.13">Job 9:13</reference>; Isa 30:7. The poet means to say that everything of which our life is proud (riches, outward appearance, luxury, beauty, etc.), when regarded in the right light, is after all only עמל, inasmuch as it causes us trouble and toil, and און, because without any true intrinsic merit and worth. To this second predicate is appended the confirmatory clause. חישׁ is <hi type="italic">infin. adverb</hi>. from חוּשׁ, הישׁ, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.35">Deu 32:35</reference> : speedily, swiftly (Symmachus, the Quinta, and Jerome). The verb גּוּז signifies <hi type="italic">transire</hi> in all the Semitic dialects; and following this signification, which is applied transitively in Num 11:31, the Jewish expositors and Schultens correctly render: <hi type="italic">nam transit velocissime</hi>. Following upon the perfect גּז, the <hi type="italic">modus consecutivus</hi> ונּעפה maintains its retrospective signification. The strengthening of this mood by means of the intentional <hi type="italic">ah</hi> is more usual with the 1st <hi type="italic">pers. sing</hi>., e.g., <reference osisRef="Gen.32.6">Gen 32:6</reference>, than with the <hi type="italic">1st pers. plur</hi>., as here and in <reference osisRef="Gen.41.11">Gen 41:11</reference>; Ew. §232, <hi type="italic">g</hi>. The poet glances back from the end of life to the course of life. And life, with all of which it had been proud, appears as an empty burden; for it passed swiftly by and we fled away, we were borne away with rapid flight upon the wings of the past. <div eID="gen9905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9906" type="x-p"/> Such experience as this ought to urge one on to the fear of God; but how rarely does this happen! and yet the fear of God is the condition (stipulation) and the beginning of wisdom. The verb ידע in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.90.11">Psa 90:11</reference></hi>, just as it in general denotes not merely notional but practically living and efficient knowledge, is here used of a knowledge which makes that which is known conduce to salvation. The meaning of וּכיראתך is determined in accordance with this. The suffix is here either <hi type="italic">gen. subj.</hi>: according to Thy fearfulness (יראה as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.18">Eze 1:18</reference>), or <hi type="italic">gen. obj.</hi>: according to the fear that is due to Thee, which in itself is at once (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.5.8">Psa 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.20.20">Exo 20:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.2.25">Deu 2:25</reference>) more natural, and here designates the knowledge which is so rarely found, as that which is determined by the fear of God, as a truly religious knowledge. Such knowledge Moses supplicates for himself and for Israel: to number our days teach us rightly to understand. <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.17">1Sa 23:17</reference>, where כּן ידע signifies “he does not know it to be otherwise, he is well aware of it,” shows how כּן is meant. Hitzig, contrary to the accentuation, draws it to למנות ימינו; but “to number our days” is in itself equivalent to “hourly to contemplate the fleeting character and brevity of our lifetime;” and כּן הודע prays for a true qualification for this, and one that accords with experience. The future that follows is well adapted to the call, as frequently aim and result. But הביא is not to be taken, with Ewald and Hitzig, in the signification of bringing as an offering, a meaning this verb cannot have of itself alone (why should it not have been ונקריב?). Böttcher also erroneously renders it after the analogy of <reference osisRef="Prov.2.10">Pro 2:10</reference> : “that we may bring wisdom into the heart,” which ought to be בּלב. הביא, deriving its meaning from agriculture, signifies “to carry off, obtain, gain, prop. to bring in,” viz., into the barn, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.10">2Sa 9:10</reference>, Hagg. <reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>; the produce of the field, and in a general way gain or profit, is hence called תּבוּאה. A wise heart is the fruit which one reaps or garners in from such numbering of the days, the gain which one carries off from so constantly reminding one’s self of the end. לבב חכמה is a poetically intensified expression for לב חכם, just as לב מרפּא in <reference osisRef="Prov.14.30">Pro 14:30</reference> signifies a calm easy heart.
entries.7398074d35f8b86c2b30d9a014d510daea2b07b8: <reference osisRef="Ps.90.13-Ps.90.17">Psa 90:13-17</reference> <div eID="gen9906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9907" type="x-p"/> The prayer for a salutary knowledge, or discernment, of the appointment of divine wrath is now followed by the prayer for the return of favour, and the wish that God would carry out His work of salvation and bless Israel’s undertakings to that end. We here recognise the well-known language of prayer of Moses in <reference osisRef="Exod.32.12">Exo 32:12</reference>, according to which שׁוּבה is not intended as a prayer for God’s return to Israel, but for the turning away of His anger; and the sigh עד־מתי that is blended with its asks how long this being angry, which threatens to blot Israel out, is still to last. והנּהם is explained according to this same parallel passage: May God feel remorse or sorrow (which in this case coincide) concerning His servants, i.e., concerning the affliction appointed to them. The naming of the church by עבדיך (as in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.27">Deu 9:27</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.32.13">Exo 32:13</reference> of the patriarchs) reminds one of <reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">Deu 32:36</reference> : <hi type="italic">concerning His servants He shall feel compassion</hi> (<hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. instead of the <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi>). The prayer for the turning of wrath is followed in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.14">Psa 90:14</reference> by the prayer for the turning towards them of favour. In בּבּקר there lies the thought that it has been night hitherto in Israel. “Morning” is therefore the beginning of a new season of favour. In שׂבּענוּ (to which הסדּך is a second accusative of the object) is implied the thought that Israel whilst under wrath has been hungering after favour; cf. the adjective שׂבע in the same tropical signification in Deu 33:23. The supplicatory imperatives are followed by two moods expressive of intention: then will we, or: in order that we may rejoice and be glad; for futures like these set forth the intention of attaining something as a result or aim of what has been expressed just before: Ew. §325, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. בּכל־ימינוּ is not governed by the verbs of rejoicing (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.24">Psa 118:24</reference>), in which case it would have been בּחיּינוּ, but is an adverbial definition of time (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.2">Psa 145:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.8">Psa 35:8</reference>): within the term of life allotted to us. We see from <reference osisRef="Ps.90.15">Psa 90:15</reference> that the season of affliction has already lasted for a long time. The duration of the forty years of wrath, which in the midst of their course seemed to them as an eternity, is made the measure of the reviving again that is earnestly sought. The plural ימות instead of ימי is common only to our Psalm and <reference osisRef="Deut.32.7">Deu 32:7</reference>; it is not known elsewhere to Biblical Hebrew. And the poetical שׁנות instead of שׁני, which also occurs elsewhere, appears for the first time in Deu 32:7. The meaning of ענּיתנוּ, in which ימות hcihw is specialized after the manner of a genitive, is explained from Deu 8:2., according to which the forty years’ wandering in the wilderness was designed to humble (ענּות) and to prove Israel through suffering. At the close of these forty years Israel stands on the threshold of the Promise Land. To Israel all final hopes were closely united with the taking possession of this land. We learn from Gen. 49 that it is the horizon of Jacob’s prophetic benediction. This Psalm too, in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.16-Ps.90.17">Psa 90:16-17</reference>, terminates in the prayer for the attainment of this goal. The psalmist has begun in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">Psa 90:1</reference> his adoration with the majestic divine name אדני; in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.13">Psa 90:13</reference> he began his prayer with the gracious divine name יהוה; and now, where he mentions God for the third time, he gives to Him the twofold name, so full of faith, אדני אלהינוּ. אל used once alternates with the thrice repeated על: salvation is not Israel’s own work, but the work of Jahve; it therefore comes from above, it comes and meets Israel. It is worthy of remark that the noun פּעל occurs only in Deuteronomy in the whole Tôra, and that here also of the gracious rule of Jahve, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.4">Psa 32:4</reference>, cf. Psa 33:11. The church calls the work of the Lord מעשׂה ידינוּ in so far as He executes it through them. This expression מעשׂה ידים as a designation of human undertakings runs through the whole of the Book of Deuteronomy: <reference osisRef="Deut.2.7">Deu 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.28">Deu 4:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.7">Deu 11:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.14.29">Deu 14:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.15">Deu 16:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.24.19">Deu 24:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.27.15">Deu 27:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.12">Deu 28:12</reference>; Deu 30:9. In the work of the Lord the bright side of His glory unveils itself, hence it is called הדר; this too is a word not alien at least to the language of Deuteronomy, Deu 33:17. Therein is made manifest נעם ה, His graciousness and condescension - an expression which David has borrowed from Moses in Psa 27:4. יראה and יהי are optatives. כּוננה is an urgent request, <hi type="italic">imperat. obsecrantis</hi> as the old expositors say. With <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> the same thought is expressed over again (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Isa 55:1</reference>, וּלכוּ, yea come) - a simple, childlike anadiplosis which vividly reminds us of the Book of Deuteronomy, which revolves in thoughts that are ever the same, and by that very means speaks deeply to the heart. Thus the Deuteronomic impression of this Psalm accompanies us from beginning to end, from מעון to מעשׂה ידים. Nor will it now be merely accidental that the fondness for comparisons, which is a peculiarity of the Book of Deuteronomy (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.31">Deu 1:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.44">Deu 1:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.8.5">Deu 8:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.29">Deu 28:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.49">Deu 28:49</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.28.13">Deu 28:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.44">Deu 28:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.29.17-Deut.29.18">Deu 29:17-18</reference>), is found again in this Psalm.  <chapter eID="Ps.90"/> <div eID="gen9907" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 90
As Moses is about to treat as well of the brevity and miseries of human life, as of the punishments inflicted upon the people of Israel, in order to minister some consolation for assuaging the grief and fear which the faithful might have entertained upon observing the operation of the common law, to which all mankind are subject, and especially, upon considering their own afflictions, he opens the psalm by speaking of the peculiar grace which God had vouchsafed to his chosen tribes. He next briefly recites, how wretched the condition of men is, if they allow their hearts to rest in this world, especially when God summons them as guilty sinners to his judgment seat. And after he has bewailed, that even the children of Abraham had experienced for a time such severity, that they were almost consumed with sorrow, confiding in God’s free favor, by which He had adopted them to himself, he prays that He would deal towards them in a merciful and gracious manner, as he had done in times past, and that he would continue even to the end the ordinary course of his grace.
A Prayer of Moses, the man of God.
It is uncertain whether this psalm was composed by Moses, or whether some one of the prophets framed it into a song for the use of the people, from a formula of prayer written by Moses, and handed down from age to age. It is, however, highly probable, that it is not without some ground ascribed to Moses in the title; and since psalms were in use even in his time, I have no doubt that he was its author.
“Pour faire la fin de ce livre troisieme.” — Fr. “As a conclusion to this third Book.” The Psalter, as we have before observed, has been divided by the Hebrews into five books. This is the end of Book 3. See volume 2, page 126, note.
Some maintain that the reason why his name appears in the inscription is, that it was sung by his posterity; but I cannot see why they should have recourse to such a groundless conceit. The epithet, The man of God, given to Moses, which is immediately added, clearly confutes them.
All the ancient versions ascribe this psalm to Moses, and it is generally agreed, that it was written by him. To him also, R. Selomo, and other Jewish commentators, ascribe the nine following psalms; for which they do not appear to have any other foundation but their own absurd canon of criticism, by which they assign all anonymous psalms to that author whose name last occurred in a preceding title. It is evident, for instance, that the 99th psalm, in which the prophet Samuel is mentioned, could not have been written by Moses.
This honorable designation is expressly applied to him, that his doctrine may have the greater authority. If conjectures are to be admitted, it is probable, that when the time of his death drew near, he endited this prayer to assuage the prolonged sorrow under which the people had almost pined away, and to comfort their hearts, under the accumulation of adversities with which they were oppressed. Although the wonderful goodness of God shone brightly in their deliverance from Egypt, which, burying the miseries formerly endured by them, might have filled them with joy; yet we know that, soon after, it was extinguished by their ingratitude; so that for the space of not less than forty years, they were consumed with continual languor in the wilderness. It was therefore very seasonable for Moses at that time to beseech God that he would deal mercifully and gently with his people, according to the number of the years in which he had afflicted them.
Psalm 90:1-2
1. O Lord! thou hast been our dwelling-place, from generation to generation. 2. Before the mountains were brought forth, and before thou hadst formed the earth and the world,
Man of God was a common designation of the Jewish prophets: comp. Judges 13:6; 1 Samuel 2:27; 9:6.
even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
 
1 O Lord! thou hast been our dwelling-place. In separating the seed of Abraham by special privilege from the rest of the human family, the Psalmist magnifies the grace of adoption, by which God had embraced them as his children. The object which he has in view in this exordium is, that God would now renew the grace which he had displayed in old time towards the holy patriarchs, and continue it towards their offspring. Some commentators think that he alludes to the tabernacle, because in it the majesty of God was not less conspicuous than if he had dwelt in the midst of the people; but this seems to me to be altogether out of place. He rather comprehends the whole time in which the Fathers sojourned in the land of Canaan. As the tabernacle had not yet continued for the space of forty years, the long duration here mentioned — our dwelling-place from generation to generation — would not at all be applicable to it. It is not then intended to recount what God showed himself to be towards the Israelites from the time that he delivered them from Egypt; but what their fathers had experienced him to be in all ages, even from the beginning.
“The earth and the world. The latter of those words properly means, the habitable world; that part of the earth which, by its fertility, is capable of supporting inhabitants.” — Walford.
Now it is declared that as they had always been pilgrims and wanderers, so God was to them instead of a dwelling-place. No doubt, the condition of all men is unstable upon earth; but we know that Abraham and his posterity were, above all others, sojourners, and as it were exiles. Since, then, they wandered in the land of Canaan till they were brought into Egypt, where they lived only by sufferance from day to day, it was necessary for them to seek for themselves a dwelling-place under the shadow of God, without which they could hardly be accounted inhabitants of the world, since they continued everywhere strangers, and were afterwards led about through many windings and turnings. The grace which the Lord displayed in sustaining them in their wanderings, and shielding them with his hand when they sojourned among savage and cruel nations, and were exposed to injurious treatment at their hands — this grace is extolled by Moses in very striking terms, when he represents God as an abode or dwelling-place to these poor fugitives who were continually wandering from one place to another in quest of lodgings. This grace he magnifies from the length of time during which it had been exercised; for God ceased not to preserve and defend them for the space of more than four hundred years, during which time they dwelt under the wings of his protection.

                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> is chan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ged.</ns0:note> groweth up <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>which is changed,</ns0:hi> either first for the worse, <ns0:hi>which passeth away,</ns0:hi> as some render the word. Which having generally affirmed here, he may seem more particularly to explain in the next Verse. Or rather second<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly for the better, as this word is sometimes used, as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 14. 7. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 40. 31. which sprouteth out of the Earth and grow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth more apparent and green and flourishing. And this inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pretation is confirmed from the next Verse, where this same word is used in this sence, where also <ns0:hi>the morning</ns0:hi> is again mentioned, and that as the time not of its decay, but of its flourishing.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down and wither<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The whole space of mans life is compared to one day, and his prosperity is confined to a part of that day and en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded in the close of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 For we <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Either, 1. we men: or rather, 2. we Israelites in this wilderness.</ns0:note> are consumed <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either naturally by the frame of our bodies, or violently by extraordinary judgments. Thou dost not suffer us to live so long as we might by the course of nature.</ns0:note> by thine anger <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Caused by our sinful state and lives.</ns0:note>, and by thy wrath are we troubled.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Thou hast set our iniquities before thee <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Thou dost not now cover or blot out or pass by our sins, as thou hast usually done to thy people; but thou dost dili<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gently search them out, and accurately observe them, as a se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vere, but righteous Judge, and art now calling us to an ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />count for them.</ns0:note>, our secret <ns0:hi>sins</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Thou dost not onely punish us for our notorious and scandalous sins, which thine honour may seem to oblige thee to do, but even for our secret lusts, the mur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />muring and unbelief and Apostasie and Idolatry of our hearts; which though hid from the eyes of men, thou hast set before thine eyes and brought them to light by thy judgments.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> at the luminary of thy countenance.</ns0:note> in the light of thy countenance.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 For all our days are <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> turned away.</ns0:note> passed away <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>turn away themselves</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>their face</ns0:hi> from us. They do not continue with us, but quickly turn their backs upon us and leave us.</ns0:note> in thy wrath: we spend our years <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> as a me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ditation.</ns0:note> as a tale <ns0:hi>that is</ns0:hi> told <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Which may a little affect us for the present, but is quickly ended and gone out of mind. Or, <ns0:hi>as a word,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 37. 2. which in an instant is gone, and that irrevoca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bly. Or, <ns0:hi>as a thought,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>a sigh,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>a breath.</ns0:hi> All which come to one sence.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. as for <ns0:hi>the days of our years in them</ns0:hi> are <ns0:hi>seventy years.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> The days of our years <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Either 1. of the Israelites in the desart, who being twen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty years old, and some thirty, some forty, some fifty years old when they came out of <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> and dying in the Wilder<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, as all of that age did, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 14. 29. a great number of them doubtless died in their seventieth or eightieth year, as is here implyed. Or rather 2. of the generality of mankind, and the Israelites no less than others, in that and all following Ages, some few persons excepted, amongst whom were <ns0:hi>Mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Caleb</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ioshua,</ns0:hi> who lived an hundred and twenty years; which is therefore noted of them as a thing singular and extraordinary. This sence suits best with the following words, and with the scope of <ns0:hi>Moses;</ns0:hi> which was to represent the vain and transitory condition of men in this life, and how much mankind was now sunk below their Ancestors, who commonly lived many hundreds of years, and that the Israe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lites, though Gods peculiar people and endowed with many priviledges, yet in this were no better than other men. All which may be considered either as an argument to move God to pity and spare them, or as a motive to awaken and quick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />en the Israelites to serious preparations for death, by com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />paring this with <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 12.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> threescore years and ten <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Which time the antient Heathen Writers also fixed as the usual space of mens lives.</ns0:note>; and if by reason of strength <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> By the strength of their natural constitution; which is the true and common cause of longer life.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>they be</ns0:hi> fourscore years, yet is their strength <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Their strongest and most vigorous old Age. Or, <ns0:hi>their excellency,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>pride;</ns0:hi> that old age which is their glory, and in which men do commonly glory.</ns0:note> la<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bour
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:487" />
and sorrow <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Filled with troubles and griefs from the infirmities of age, the approach of Death, and the contingences of humane life.</ns0:note>: for it <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Either our age, or our strength.</ns0:note> is soon cut off <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">It doth not now de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cline by many degrees and slow steps, as it doth in our young and flourishing age, but decayeth apace and suddenly fleeth away.</ns0:note>, and we flee away <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">We do not now go to Death, as we do from our very Birth, nor run, but flee swiftly away like a Bird, as this word signifies.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Who knoweth <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Few or none sufficiently apprehend it or stedfastly be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve it, or duly consider it, or are rightly affected with it. For all these things are comprehended under this word <ns0:hi>know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> the power of thine an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The greatness and force and dreadful effects of thine anger conceived against the Sons of men, and in particular a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst thine own people for their miscarriages.</ns0:note>? even according to thy fear <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to the fear of thee, as <ns0:hi>my fear</ns0:hi> is put for <ns0:hi>the fear of me, Mal.</ns0:hi> 1. 6. and <ns0:hi>his knowledge</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>the knowledge of him, Isa.</ns0:hi> 53. 11. According to that fear or dread which sinful men have of a just and holy God. These fears of the Deity are not vain Bugbears, and the effects of ignorance and folly or Su<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perstition, as Heathens and Atheists have sometimes said, but are just and built upon solid grounds and justified by the ter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rible effects of thy wrath upon mankind.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>so is</ns0:hi> thy wrath <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">It bears full pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />portion to it, nay indeed doth far exceed it. It cannot be said of Gods wrath which is said of Death, that the fear of it is worse than the thing it self. But this Verse is by many both antient and later Interpreters rendred otherwise, and that very agreeably to the Hebrew Text, <ns0:hi>who knoweth the power of thine anger, and thy wrath according to thy fear?</ns0:hi> i. e. either 1. according to the fear of thee, or so as thou art to be feared, or answerably to thy terrible displeasure against sin and sinners. Or 2. so as to fear and dread thee in such manner and measure as sinful Creatures ought to fear the in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />finite and offended Majesty of God their Creator and Judge and Soveraign, and thereby to be moved to humble himself before thee and fervently to seek thy face and favour; which is the onely true wisdom, for which he prayeth in the next Verse.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 39. 4.</ns0:note> So teach us <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">By thy spirit and grace as thou hast already taught us by thy word. Or, <ns0:hi>Teach us rightly</ns0:hi> (as this word is used <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 27. 7. and 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 7. 9.) <ns0:hi>to number,</ns0:hi> &c. as it follows.</ns0:note> to number our days <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">To consider the shortness and miseries of this life, and the cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tainty and speediness of Death, and the causes and conse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quences thereof.</ns0:note>, that we may <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> cause to come.</ns0:note> apply <ns0:hi>our</ns0:hi> hearts unto wisdom <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That we may heartily devote our selves to the study and practice of true wisdom, which is nothing else but piety or the fear of God. And why so? Not that the Israelites might thereby procure a revocation of that perem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ptory sentence of death passed upon all that Generation; nor that other men might hereby prevent their death, both which he very well knew to be impossible, but that men might arm and prepare themselves for death, and for their great account after death, and might make sure of the happi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of the future life. Of which this Text is a plain and pregnant proof.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Return, O LORD <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">To us in mercy; for thou seemest to have forsaken us and cast us off.</ns0:note>, how long <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Understand, <ns0:hi>wilt thou be angry:</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>will it be ere thou return to us.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>! and let it repent thee concerning thy servants <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Of thy severe proceedings against us, and change thy course and carriage to us.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 O satisfie us early <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Speedily, or seasonably before we be utterly con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sumed.</ns0:note> with thy mercy; that we may rejoyce, and be glad all our days.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 Make us glad according to the days <ns0:hi>where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in</ns0:hi> thou hast afflicted us, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> the years <ns0:hi>wherein</ns0:hi> we have seen evil <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Our afflictions have been sharp and long, let not our prosperity be small and short.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 Let thy work appear unto thy servants, and thy glory unto their children <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Let that great and glorious work of giving thy people a compleat deliverance, which thou hast long since designed and promised, be at last accomplished and manifested unto us, and in the sight of the World.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And let the beauty of the LORD <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> His favourable countenance and gracious influence and glorious presence.</ns0:note> our God be upon us, and establish thou the work of our hands upon us <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>in us.</ns0:hi> Do not onely work for us but in us. And because the glorious work of thy hands is hindered by the evil works of our hands, be thou pleased by thy holy spirit to <ns0:hi>direct</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>establish</ns0:hi> (for this Hebrew word signifies both) <ns0:hi>the works of our hands,</ns0:hi> that we may cease to do evil and learn to do well, and turn and constantly cleave unto thee, and not revolt and draw back from thee, as we have frequently done to our own undoing.</ns0:note>, yea the work of our hands establish thou it.</ns0:p>

                      A Prayer of Moses the man of God Who considering that terrible but righteous sentence of God concerning the cutting off all that sinful Generation in the Wilderness, of which see Numb. 14. takes that occasion to publish these Meditations concerning mans mortality and misery in this life, which might be useful both to that and to all succeeding Generations..
